thread.title: Dividend Growth Investing For Retirees? Absolutely - Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSEARCA:VIG)

author: Dale Roberts
title: Dividend Growth Investing For Retirees? Absolutely - Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (NYSEARCA:VIG)
text:
Many embrace Dividend Growth Investing for the potential of better risk-adjusted returns. If we can get the returns of the broad market with the same risk or lesser risk, then most of us will take that offer. We even might accept that we will underperform the market in times of a roaring bull market for the potential to outperform through bear markets or periods of great volatility.
That's certainly why I embraced the Dividend Achievers. I planned my portfolio construction well in advance of my life changes. I knew that I would eventually leave the full-time working world to launch my freelance writing career that includes writing on Seeking Alpha, on my new blog and writing for other well-known blogs such as Tangerine Forward Thinking .
In the retirement or semi-retirement stage, the focus turns to creating generous but durable income. And from my research, the most durable income comes by way of cash dividends and bond income in concert with the share harvesting (homemade dividends) of higher-quality companies. I found my basket of higher-quality US companies in the Dividend Achievers Index - Vanguard refers to the index using the term Dividend Appreciation.
I often write that a meaningful dividend growth history is a divining rod that can find higher-quality companies with greater financial stability and at times thanks to a wider moat. Now, to throw some water on that fire, have a read of the Sure Dividend post on the US Broad Dividend Achievers Index.
And here's the chart that shows the drastic underperformance of the US Broad Achievers versus SPY.
And yet, here's the more focused Dividend Achievers Index that applies financial filters removing some 100 companies from the US Broad Achievers list.
Portfolio 1 is the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF ( VIG ); Portfolio 2 is the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF ( IVV ).
We see that the Dividend Appreciation Fund outperforms the overall broad market S&P 500 for the full period, but most importantly through that last major market correction, when a retiree would have benefited from that lesser drawdown.
On Sure Dividend, Ben thought the underperformance of the US Broad Dividend Achievers Index Fund was due to being overvalued, but there is no data available for P/E levels of the time. The performance of VIG versus the US Broad Achievers ( PFM ) suggest that it's the filters or exclusion of more lesser caps that leads to the better performance of VIG. This dividend conundrum will be the focus of an article where we'll bring in Ben and, perhaps, Canadian portfolio modeller Kurtis Hemmerling .
VIG Outperformed When It Mattered In the correction of 2008-2009, VIG was down by 41%, while the broad market was down by some 51%, according to Portfolio Visualizer. VIG is Portfolio 1.
And the dividend income held up much better in VIG versus IVV. Once again, VIG is Portfolio 1 and IVV is Portfolio 2. The following is based on an initial investment of $10,000. The starting yield for VIG was 1.6%.
That lesser volatility and greater income durability would have greatly assisted the retiree that caught an unfortunate retirement start date. With an initial $100,000 at a 4% annual spend rate, inflation-adjusted, we see VIG hold up much better than "the market" for retirement funding.
That said, watching your portfolio (perhaps a significant portion of your liquid wealth) fall by some 40% is not every retiree's cup of tea. Some bonds or shock absorbers might be in order.
From my research, the Balanced Growth model might be the sweet spot for retirees. It's still an aggressive mix for a retiree, but it might deliver when one seeks to maximize the income potential of a portfolio.
Portfolio 1 is VIG at 70% and Mid Term Treasuries ( IEF ) at 30%; Portfolio 2 is IVV with no bond support.
We see that the Dividend Achievers Balanced Growth Portfolio is already back in positive territory even after paying out 4% annual, inflation-adjusted.
And to apply a fair benchmark comparison, here's Portfolio 2 as IVV at 70% and IEF at 30%. Both portfolios now have the same stock-to-bond ratio.
Advantage Dividend Achievers.
And what about the 2000-2002 market correction? When we go back and look at the worst start date for retirees, I like to bring this article to the table: " How Retirees Made It Through The Last 2 Recessions ."
One approach that worked was a simple mix of larger-cap dividend-paying companies, some international equity exposure and some bonds - that Balanced Portfolio.
A retiree might help their odds by embracing an ever-greater and more meaningful dividend growth history in the large cap space by way of Dividend Aristocrats ( NOBL ).
Here's the annual returns history of the Dividend Aristocrats from 1990, thanks to Seeking Alpha author Ploutos.
We see positive performance in 2000 and 2001, when the S&P 500 was now two-thirds of the way through that negative performance hat-trick - down 3 years in a row. That hat-trick has only occurred in one other period for US stocks. 2000 was more than a rough period for retirees.
While many will cry that looking that the Dividend Aristocrats in the rear-view mirror is reverse-engineered data mining, I'd suggest that the filter is quite simple. We're looking at larger-cap and very liquid S&P 500 constituents that have a history of increasing their dividend every year for 25 years or more.
Once again (and back to that Dividend Achievers conundrum), we might be back to the magic mix, including a meaningful dividend growth history and a larger-cap bias. That larger-cap addition might be delivering more established and more sustainable business models - more moat.
My retirement monies are on Dividend Growth. In 2015, I skimmed 15 of the largest-cap Achievers that includes 9 Aristocrats. For Canadian companies, I hold a concentrate basket of dividend payers that offer a wider moat. I throw some bonds into the mix.
What about living off of the dividend income? Many will suggest that it's easier and "better" to live off of the dividend income and to boost the income to the desired level. On that I will offer that the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF ( VYM ) performed worse than the S&P 500 for retirees through the last recession.
Retirement success mostly comes down to the growth and quality of the companies that you hold, not the yield. Other higher income yield-chasing assets were crushed in the last recession. Retirees were crushed.
Again, my money is on that divining rod of Dividend Growth digging in the large-cap space, paying little attention to the dividend yield.
